## Abstract

This paper focuses on the context of China and examines the allocation and effects on aggregate TFP of Government Venture Capital (Government VC) using linked firm-level and supply-chain data. I find that in China, Government VC accounts for approximately 10% of the venture capital market and targets strategic sectors, including semiconductors, with high Domar weights, substantial import dependence, and scope for innovation and learning by doing. Within sectors, Government VC-backed firms together with their suppliers and buyers have broader buyer networks and higher innovation intensity than firms without VC backing or those backed by private VC. To understand the firm-level effect of Government VC investment, I adopted a staggered difference-in-differences design, and I find that Government VC increases funded firms’ sales by 14.5%, wage bill by 12.8%, and capital by 15.1% on average within 2 years. The effects spread through production networks: suppliers’ sales increase by 2.5%, wage bill increases by 2.7%, capital increases by 1.5% on average within 2 years, and buyers’ sales increase by 4.1%, wage bill increases by 3.6%, capital increases by 1.2% on average within 2 years. These patterns are consistent with propagation through supply and demand linkages. Aggregating the estimated effects in a Baqaee–Farhi production-network framework, I find that Government VC raises manufacturing aggregate TFP by 0.07%, equivalent to approximately RMB 14.51 billion in the 2016 benchmark economy, driven by factor reallocation. As a case of discretionary industrial policy, Government VC demonstrates how targeting improves aggregate efficiency through improving resource allocation efficiency in the short run.
